textbookText: Figure 8.3.13 excretory system in earthworm 1. Pharyngeal nephridia Pharyngeal nephridia are found as paired tufts on the both side of pharynx and oesophagus in the 4th, 5th and 6th segment. Each tuft comprises hundreds of coiled branched tubules along with blood glands. In each tuft, a single thick-walled common duct is formed by the union of the terminal duct of all nephridia. This nephridial duct from each tuft runs anteriorly parallel to the ventral nerve cord. Ducts of 4th and 5th segments open into pharynx while those of 6th segment open into buccal chamber or 2nd segment. Pharyngeal nephridia are enteronephric nephridia or endonephric as they pour waste into the alimentary canal i.e. pharynx and buccal cavity through the common nephridial duct. These nephridia are closed type i.e. without nephrostome and they extract waste from only capillaries. 2. Integumentary nephridia These nephridia are found distributed on the entire inner surface of body wall except first two segments. About 200-250 nephridia are found in each segment except clitellum region. Each segment of clitellar region contains about 2000-2500 integumentary nephridia. So the clitellar region is also called “forest of nephridia”. Integumentary nephridia are microscopic, V-shaped and without nephrostome or any opening into coelom. Hence, they are closed type nephridia. The terminal duct of each nephridium opens exteriorly through the minute opening called nephridiopore on the outer surface of the body wall. These nephridia discharge wastes directly to the outside and hence called exonephric or ectonephric nephridia. These nephridia also extract wastes from capillaries only. 3. Septal nephridia Septal nephridia are the largest and considered as the most advanced or typical nephridia of earthworm with the nephrostome. They are found attached to both the faces of each intersegmental septum behind 15th segment. Altogether 80-100 septal nephridia are found on each septum except 15th segment which contains only 40-50. Septal nephridia remain Biology, Grade 11 | 368

suspended freely in coelomic chambers. They are called enteronephric since they also discharge wastes into the gut. Each septal nephridium consists of 3 parts: i. Nephrostome or nephridiostome It is the proximal, ciliated funnel like structure, communicating with coelom. Nephrostome consists of an oval shaped pore bounded by ciliated upper lip and lower lip. Upper lip consists of about eight ciliated marginal cells and a large central cell and lower lip is lined with about four ciliated compact cells. Continuous beating movement of these cilia helps to extract nitrogenous wastes from coelomic fluid.

Figure 8.3.14 A septal nephridium in earthworm ii. Body A short, thin and ciliated tube called neck connects the nephrostome with the main body of nephridium. Body consists of two parts- a short straight lobe, and a long-twisted loop with a narrow apical lobe. Twisted lobe consists of a proximal limb and a distal limb which are spirally twisted upon each other. Number of twists varies from 9-13. Proximal limb is joined to the neck. iii. Terminal duct Figure 8.3.15 T.S. of Terminal duct Distal limb of body of nephridium posteriorly gives off a short and narrow duct called terminal duct. Terminal ducts of all septal nephridia open into the septal excretory canals of either side.

There are two supra intestinal ducts extending length wise from 15th segment up to the last segment dorsally above the intestine. Each septal excretory canal leads into supra-intestinal excretory ducts of its own side. Finally, supra-intestinal excretory ducts open into the lumen of intestine in each segment through narrow ductules, each having a sphinctered opening. The lumen of nephridium contains ciliated canals, which are four within straight lobe, three in proximal limb and distal limb each, two in apical lobe, and one in neck and terminal duct. In this way, wastes collected by septal nephridia are discharged first into septal excretory canals through terminal ducts and then passed to supra-intestinal excretory ducts, from where wastes are passed into the intestinal lumen and expelled out through the anus. Physiology of excretion In general, earthworm excretes 40% ammonia, 50% urea, 0.6% amino-acid and remaining other compound in excretory fluid. A well-fed earthworm excretes comparatively more ammonia in excretory fluid whereas starved one excretes more urea. Gland cells in pharyngeal and integumentary nephridia extract nitrogenous wastes and water from the blood. Integumentary nephridia discharge waste directly to outside through the pores in their body surface. Pharyngeal nephridia discharge waste to the alimentary canal from where wastes are expelled out through anus. Septal nephridia have ciliated nephrostome. Continous beating of cilia extracts wastes from the coelomic fluid which is later poured into alimentary canal and eliminated with faeces.
